analogy.p: Imagine a popular school that suddenly doubles its intake overnight. There are not enough desks, classrooms or teachers, so some pupils end up squeezed into corridors and borrowed spaces. Rio is similar: migrants arrived faster than homes and services could be built, so many 'squeezed' into hillside favelas, and the city has had to catch up by adding services afterwards. The analogy breaks down because pupils are placed by the school, while migrants choose where to live and the favelas became communities with their own businesses and culture that the city cannot simply 'rebuild'.
analogy.t: A school with too many new pupils

bullets: Case-study questions are usually 4 or 6 marks and often carry **SPaG marks** in the 9-mark extended question on Paper 2, so accurate named detail (places, schemes, figures) is what lifts an answer into the top level.
The command words most often attached are **Describe**, **Explain**, **Assess** and **To what extent**; the last two need a judgement, not just a list.
Always name Rio's districts and schemes (Rocinha, Favela-Bairro, Barra da Tijuca, Guanabara Bay) rather than writing 'the city' or 'the slums'.
Use a figure when you can, but only one you are sure of. Approximate language ('about 22%', 'over 6 million') is safer than a precise number you half-remember.
Structure to learn: Location > Importance > Causes of growth > Opportunities (social, economic) > Challenges (slums, services, jobs and crime, environment) > Planning scheme > Evaluation.
This point links forward to sustainable urban living (geo.3.4) and back to causes of urban growth (geo.3.1): the push-pull and natural-increase ideas explain Rio's growth.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: AQA GCSE Geography (8035), Urban issues and challenges, requires a case study of **one major city in a lower income country (LIC) or newly emerging economy (NEE)**. You must be able to use it to illustrate seven things: its **location and importance** (regionally, nationally and internationally), the **causes of its growth** (natural increase and migration), the **opportunities** that growth has created (social and economic), the **challenges** that growth has created (managing growth, services, jobs and crime, environmental issues), and **one example of urban planning that improves quality of life for the urban poor**. These notes use **Rio de Janeiro, Brazil** (Brazil is an NEE); if your school taught Mumbai, Lagos or another city, use the same framework but your own place-specific facts, because examiners reward the case study you were taught.

bullets: Brazil is classed as an **NEE** (newly emerging economy): rapid industrial growth, rising GDP and a growing middle class, but very large inequality.
The city proper has a population of about **6.7 million**, while the wider metropolitan area has well over **12 million**, making it Brazil's second-largest urban area after São Paulo.
Rio was Brazil's **capital until 1960**, when the capital moved inland to Brasília; it kept its prestige and many headquarters.
It is a **port city** with a natural deep-water harbour at Guanabara Bay, which made it a trading hub for coffee, sugar and (historically) gold and enslaved people.

Districts are often described as: the wealthy **Zona Sul** (south, e.g. Copacabana, Ipanema), the newer wealthy **Barra da Tijuca** (west), the central business district (**Centro**), and the poorer **Zona Norte** (north) plus the far west.
In an exam, a sketch map or description should mention the coast, the bay, the hills and the neighbouring cities of the state.
core.h: Location and setting of Rio de Janeiro
core.p: Rio de Janeiro is on the **south-east coast of Brazil**, on the Atlantic Ocean beside **Guanabara Bay**, in the state of Rio de Janeiro. The city sits on a narrow strip of low land squeezed between the sea and steep granite mountains (Sugar Loaf, Corcovado, the Tijuca massif). This physical setting is geographically important: there is very little flat, safe, easily built land, so the poorest migrants ended up building informal homes on the steep hillsides above the wealthy areas, which is exactly why **favelas** are so visible in Rio.

bullets: **Regional:** state capital; main port and transport hub for south-east Brazil; commuters from the surrounding metropolitan area (Niterói, Duque de Caxias and others) work in the city.

**Regional/national:** the country's **oil industry** is centred here; offshore oilfields in the Campos and Santos basins are managed from Rio, and Petrobras (the national oil company) is based in the city.
**National:** Brazil's second-largest city; headquarters of major companies and of TV Globo (Brazil's largest media company); centre of culture such as **Carnival**, samba and football.
**National:** one of the main sources of tourist income in Brazil; a major financial and services centre.
**International:** hosted the **1992 UN Earth Summit**, the **2014 FIFA World Cup final** and the **2016 Summer Olympics**, the first Olympics in South America.
**International:** the statue of **Christ the Redeemer** (named one of the New Seven Wonders of the World in 2007) and beaches such as Copacabana make Rio a globally recognised tourism brand.
Link: this importance is a **pull factor** - it is why migrants from poorer rural regions continue to move to Rio.
core.h: Importance of Rio: regional, national and international
core.p: The spec specifically asks for importance at **three scales**, and good answers label each one. Regionally, Rio is the **capital and economic centre of its state**, with a huge workforce commuting from surrounding towns. Nationally, it is one of Brazil's two great cities, a centre of media, finance, oil and tourism. Internationally, it is a global tourist destination and has hosted world-class events, which gives it a place in the global network of cities.

bullets: **Push factors:** rural poverty, drought and crop failure in the north-east, mechanisation of farming, shortage of land, few schools and hospitals, poor wages.
**Pull factors:** more jobs (factories, construction, services, informal work), higher wages, better access to education and healthcare, the glamour and opportunity attached to a famous city.

**Natural increase** = birth rate minus death rate. Migrants are mostly aged 15-35, so crude birth rate in poor districts is high, while improved healthcare lowers the death rate; the gap drives growth.
**Industrialisation and globalisation** (oil, shipbuilding, services, tourism, events) drew in investment and jobs, which strengthened the pull of Rio.
Growth was fastest in the **mid-20th century**; today growth is slower and more of it comes from natural increase and movement within the metropolitan area.
Examiners reward the **linking sentence**: 'Young migrants moved to Rio, had children there, so natural increase added to migration, making population grow even faster.'
Exam tip: do not say 'people move because the city is nicer'. Say **why** in specific terms (jobs, wages, services) and **name** a push from the north-east.
core.h: Causes of growth: migration and natural increase
core.p: Rio grew rapidly through the 20th century because of two processes that you must always name together: **rural-urban migration** and **natural increase**. Migrants moved from poorer regions, especially the drought-prone **north-east of Brazil** and rural areas where farm mechanisation removed jobs, because Rio offered jobs, services and hope of a better life. Because migrants are mostly young adults, they then have children in the city, which produces high natural increase and makes the city grow even when migration slows.

bullets: **Access to education:** many more schools, colleges and universities in Rio than in rural areas, so migrants' children usually have a better chance of schooling and higher literacy.
**Access to healthcare:** more hospitals, clinics and specialist care, which helps lower infant mortality and raises life expectancy.

**Access to water and energy:** a larger share of people in Rio have piped water and electricity than in remote rural areas, partly because infrastructure (like pipes and cables) reaches more people per kilometre.
**Culture, leisure and sport:** festivals, music, football, beaches and public space create social life and cultural identity (for example Carnival and samba schools that bring communities together).
**Improved infrastructure:** hosting the World Cup and Olympics brought investment in transport (metro extension, bus rapid transit, light rail) that benefits many residents.
**Remittances and social mobility:** some migrants earn enough to send money back to rural families or move into better housing over time.
Evaluation: the opportunities are **unevenly shared**; richer districts benefit most, while many favela residents lack full access to services.
core.h: Social opportunities created by urban growth
core.p: Urban growth is not only a problem; the spec asks for the **opportunities** it has created. Social opportunities mean improvements to people's lives through services and resources. Because so many people are concentrated in one place, it is cheaper and more efficient to provide services per person (an **economy of scale**) than in the scattered countryside, so Rio offers a greater range of schools, hospitals and utilities than most rural parts of Brazil.

bullets: **Industrial development:** oil and gas, shipbuilding, steel and chemicals, supported by the port and by the oil fields offshore.
**Services and tourism:** hotels, restaurants, shops, transport and entertainment employ many people, especially because of beaches, Carnival and global events.
**Formal employment:** office jobs, factory jobs, public sector jobs; they provide steady wages and taxes that the city can use for services.

**Informal employment:** many favela residents earn a living selling food or goods, repairing items, recycling waste or working as cleaners and drivers; it is flexible but insecure, with no tax, sick pay or protection.
**Multiplier effect:** wages earned in the city are spent locally, creating more demand and more jobs.
**Investment and regeneration:** events brought investment in areas such as the port district (**Porto Maravilha**).
Compare: formal jobs provide security and pay tax; informal jobs give income but lack protection - a classic comparison point in 6-mark answers.
core.h: Economic opportunities created by urban growth
core.p: Economic opportunities are the jobs and income that city growth creates. A large urban population provides both a **big workforce** and a **big market of customers**, which attracts businesses. In Rio this includes **formal employment** (registered jobs with contracts and tax) and a very large **informal sector** (unregistered work such as street vending, waste-picking and domestic work).

bullets: **Squatter settlement:** homes built on land the residents do not legally own; **slum:** overcrowded, poor-quality housing with few services; these overlap, and the spec uses both words.
Houses are often made from **brick, scrap wood and corrugated iron**, built close together on steep slopes, so they are vulnerable to **landslides** during heavy rain and to fire.
Overcrowding and poor ventilation spread disease; many early favelas had **no sewers, piped water or legal electricity**.
Because residents had no legal title, they could not use their home as security for a loan and could be evicted; this discouraged investment in the homes.
Inequality is visible: favelas sit just metres from wealthy areas like Zona Sul, which feeds social tension.
Favelas are not only problems: they have strong community spirit, local businesses and are close to jobs, which is why many residents do not want to move far away.
Link to the planning example: governments eventually chose to **upgrade** rather than demolish.
core.h: Challenge 1: managing urban growth - slums and squatter settlements
core.p: The biggest visible challenge is housing. Migrants arrived faster than the city could build homes, so many built their own on any available land, usually **steep hillsides** or flood-prone areas, without permission. These are called **favelas** in Brazil (generic terms are **slums**, **squatter settlements** or **shanty towns**). About **one in five** Rio residents (roughly 22% in the 2010 census, around 1.4 million people) live in favelas. Rocinha is the best-known, with tens of thousands of residents.

bullets: **Clean water:** many homes rely on shared standpipes or illegal connections; contaminated water spreads cholera, typhoid and diarrhoea.
**Sanitation:** open drains and sewage running through streets; it is also a problem for the wider city because untreated sewage flows to Guanabara Bay.
**Energy:** informal 'gatos' (illegal connections) are dangerous and unreliable.
**Health:** overcrowding, poor sanitation and pollution lead to higher rates of respiratory disease, dengue and tuberculosis.
**Education:** too few school places and teachers in poor areas, so many children leave early and take informal jobs.
**Cost and access:** narrow, steep alleys make it hard to lay pipes or reach homes with ambulances and bin lorries.
Services are improved by programmes such as Favela-Bairro (water, sewers, paved streets, community centres).
core.h: Challenge 2: providing clean water, sanitation, energy, health and education
core.p: The second challenge is providing **basic services** for rapidly growing, informal districts. Infrastructure is expensive and hard to install on steep, unplanned hillsides, and without legal land titles authorities were reluctant to invest. As a result, many favela residents have historically lacked **safe water, sewage systems, reliable electricity, rubbish collection, schools and clinics**, which harms health and life chances.

bullets: **Unemployment** is higher among young adults, particularly those without secondary education or with an address in a stigmatised favela.
**Informal sector:** street vendors, waste-pickers, domestic cleaners; workers lack contracts, insurance and sick pay and are easily exploited.
**Crime:** drug trafficking and violent crime are concentrated in some poorer districts; police operations have caused many deaths and a climate of fear.

**Pacification (UPP)** from 2008: permanent police units were placed in selected favelas to retake them from gangs; crime fell in some areas at first, but results were mixed and violence returned in some places.
**Stigma:** employers may discriminate against people from favelas, trapping families in a cycle of poverty.
Link: poor education > poor jobs > low income > poor housing > poor services > poor health, a cycle of deprivation that planning tries to break.
core.h: Challenge 3: unemployment, informal work and crime
core.p: Even though Rio creates many jobs, there are not enough **formal** jobs for everyone, so unemployment and underemployment are common, especially among young people in favelas. Informal work is insecure, low paid and untaxed, which means the city collects less tax to invest in services. Poverty, inequality and lack of opportunity combined with weak policing in some areas have allowed **drug gangs** to control some favelas, producing high levels of violence.

bullets: **Waste disposal:** Rio's huge landfill at **Jardim Gramacho** (once among the largest in Latin America) closed in 2012; waste-pickers who lived off it lost their livelihoods. Rubbish in favelas is often uncollected, blocking drains and increasing flood risk.
**Water pollution:** untreated sewage and industrial waste flow into **Guanabara Bay**; clean-up targets for the 2016 Olympics were not fully met.
**Air pollution:** exhaust fumes from cars, buses and industry, particularly in central areas; the surrounding hills can trap pollution.
**Traffic congestion:** rapid growth in car ownership and limited road space between the mountains and the sea cause gridlock and long commuting times.
**Loss of green space:** informal settlements and sprawl encroach on forest such as the Tijuca area.
Responses include new **Metro lines, bus rapid transit (BRT) and light rail** built around the 2014 and 2016 events, and waste and sewage schemes.
core.h: Challenge 4: environmental issues - waste, pollution and congestion
core.p: Rapid growth places huge pressure on the environment. More people means more **rubbish, sewage, traffic and emissions**, and the city's setting between mountains and bay makes some problems worse. The spec specifically lists waste disposal, air and water pollution and traffic congestion, so you should be able to give one Rio example for each.

bullets: **Aims:** integrate favelas into the formal city; improve living conditions; reduce crime and disease; give residents legal rights.

**Main features:** paved and lit streets, **piped water and sewers**, rubbish collection, drainage, **community centres, nurseries and sports facilities**, legalised electricity, and in some cases **legal land titles** and street addresses.

**Benefits:** better health (cleaner water, fewer diseases), safer streets, more investment by residents in their homes, easier access for ambulances and bin lorries, a formal address that helps getting jobs and credit.
**Cable car (Complexo do Alemão):** gave residents quick access to a rail station and the city centre, saving travel time and connecting them to jobs.

**Limitations:** often under-funded; some projects were not maintained; not all favelas were covered; improved areas can become more expensive (gentrification); crime remained a problem in some places.
**Sustainable?** Because it works with the community and is relatively cheap, it is more sustainable than demolition and relocation to distant high-rise estates.
In an exam: describe the **features**, explain **how it improves quality of life**, then make a **judgement** about how successful it has been.
core.h: Urban planning to improve the lives of the urban poor: Favela-Bairro and upgrading
core.p: The spec asks for **one example of urban planning that is improving quality of life for the urban poor**. In Rio the best-known example is the **Favela-Bairro project** (started in the 1990s), which aimed to turn favelas into regular neighbourhoods ('bairro' means neighbourhood) rather than demolishing them. The key idea is **self-help and upgrading**: the authorities provide basic infrastructure and services, while residents keep and improve their own homes. Later programmes such as the **Complexo do Alemão cable car** (2011) and **UPP policing** extended this approach.

bullets: **For the view that it is positive:** economic growth, global profile, better services than in rural areas, cultural vitality, improvements in transport and regeneration.
**For the view that it is negative:** slums, unequal access to services, pollution, informal work, crime and traffic congestion.
**Scale and time:** conditions have improved in upgraded favelas, but new informal settlements keep appearing as the population grows.
**Who benefits:** wealthier areas (Zona Sul, Barra) benefit most; poor residents benefit least, so inequality persists.
**Judgement phrase:** 'Overall, although growth has created opportunities, the challenges are greater for the urban poor because ...' and support it with a named example.
Always give a **conclusion** in 6-mark 'assess' answers; without it you cannot reach the top level.
core.h: Evaluating the impact of urban growth in Rio
core.p: The highest-level answers do not just list good and bad points; they **weigh** them. Urban growth in Rio has produced real opportunities (jobs, services, culture and investment) but its benefits are **unequally distributed**, and rapid, unplanned growth has created severe challenges for the poorest residents and for the environment. Planning has improved conditions in many areas, but inequality and violence remain.

bullets: **Contrast with UK:** UK cities grow slowly and have problems like deindustrialisation and regeneration; Rio's growth is rapid and driven by migration and natural increase.
**Link to development:** Rio shows the unequal outcomes of NEE growth: a high GDP but with huge inequality (Gini concept).
**Link to environment:** the environmental issues relate to climate change, flooding and landslides, which affect the poor most.
**For 4-mark 'explain' answers:** use point > development > link (because ...) twice.
**For 6-mark answers:** include at least two named places or schemes and a conclusion.
**For data questions:** use the 'Rio' favela figure (about 22% of residents) to show how large the challenge is and then explain its causes.
If a question asks for a different city (for example one 'in an LIC'), adapt the same framework; do not just write everything you know.
core.h: Link to other topics and exam technique for this case study
core.p: This case study links across the course. It applies the **push-pull** and **natural increase** ideas from the causes of urban growth; it is a contrast to the **UK city** case study (change and regeneration in a high-income country); and it feeds into **sustainable urban living** and into the **changing economic world** topics (NEEs, TNCs, inequality). Examiners often ask you to compare the challenges of an LIC/NEE city with a UK city, so knowing the contrast is valuable.

exam: **Describe (2-4 marks):** make separate, factual points about Rio ('Rio is on the south-east coast of Brazil next to Guanabara Bay'); one mark per point, no explanation needed.

**Explain (4 marks):** point > development > link. E.g. 'Many migrants moved from the north-east because of drought (1) which destroyed crops and left farmers without income (1), so they moved to Rio for jobs (1) ...'.

**Assess/To what extent (6 marks):** give both opportunities and challenges, use named places, compare their importance, and end with a judgement; use phrases such as 'however', 'whereas' and 'overall'.

**Case-study 9-mark questions (SPaG):** plan three paragraphs (e.g. opportunities, challenges, planning), include place detail in each, and write a clear conclusion; check spelling of favela, Rocinha, Guanabara and Rio.
**Use 'location and importance' structure:** regional (state capital, port, commuters), national (oil, media, culture, second city), international (Olympics 2016, World Cup 2014, tourism).
**Always link causes to effects:** 'rapid migration > not enough housing > squatter settlements > landslide and disease risk'.
**Evaluate planning:** consider who benefits, cost, sustainability and whether it solves the underlying problem (inequality, unemployment).
**Data questions:** if given a table of urban growth or favela populations, quote figures with units and describe the trend (increase, decrease, how fast) before explaining.
**Do not copy your case study as a script.** Answer the question asked, e.g. if it asks about environmental challenges, do not list crime or housing.
**Time management:** about 1 mark per minute; 6 marks is roughly 6-7 minutes.

mistakes.r: Name districts, schemes and places, e.g. Rocinha, Favela-Bairro, Guanabara Bay, Barra da Tijuca.
mistakes.w: Writing about 'Brazil' or 'South America' in general instead of Rio specifics.

mistakes.r: Name push factors (drought in the north-east, mechanisation) and pull factors (jobs, schools, hospitals).
mistakes.w: Saying people move to Rio 'for a better life' with no detail.

mistakes.r: The spec requires opportunities and challenges; include social and economic opportunities and judge the balance.
mistakes.w: Giving only negative points about urban growth.

mistakes.r: Favela-Bairro upgrades in place: services, paved streets, legal titles; demolition was largely rejected.
mistakes.w: Saying favelas are demolished and everyone is moved out.

mistakes.r: Natural increase = birth rate minus death rate; migration is movement of people. Both cause growth and are linked.
Finish with a clear judgement using 'overall', 'however' and a supported reason to reach top level marks.
mistakes.w: Writing an 'assess' answer without a conclusion or judgement.

mistakes.r: Use approximate, reliable figures ('over 6 million', 'about 22% in favelas') or none at all.
mistakes.w: Stating exact figures you are unsure of (e.g. invented population numbers).

mistakes.r: Say what was done, how it improved quality of life, and its limitations (funding, crime, gentrification).
mistakes.w: Using the planning example only to describe, not evaluate.

summary: The spec asks you to use one case study of a major city in an LIC or NEE (here Rio de Janeiro) to show its location and importance, why it grew (migration and natural increase), the social and economic opportunities and the challenges of growth (slums, services, jobs and crime, environment), and one planning scheme improving life for the urban poor. It matters because it is the main source of place-specific evidence in Paper 2 extended answers.

worked.ans: Rio de Janeiro is the capital of the state of Rio de Janeiro and the main port and economic centre of south-east Brazil (1). Nationally, it is Brazil's second-largest city, was its capital until 1960 and is the centre of the oil industry (Petrobras) and of the media company TV Globo (1). Internationally, it is a major tourist destination with attractions such as Christ the Redeemer and Copacabana beach (1) and it hosted the 2016 Olympic Games and the 2014 World Cup final (1).

worked.ans: Migrants arrived in Rio faster than formal housing could be built (1), so many built informal homes called favelas on steep hillsides such as Rocinha (1). These areas lacked sewers and piped water at first (1), which spread disease, and the steep, poorly built homes are at risk of landslides in heavy rain (1).
worked.q: Explain how rapid urban growth has created challenges for people living in a city in an LIC or NEE. (4 marks)
steps: Develop it: why did it happen and what is the effect?
Link to a second challenge: services/health.

worked.ans: Favela-Bairro aimed to upgrade favelas rather than demolish them by adding paved streets, piped water, sewers and community centres (1). This has improved health because clean water and drains reduce diseases such as typhoid (2), and a formal address and better access helps residents find work (1). However, funding was limited, not every favela was included, and crime and unemployment remained a problem in some places, so the poorest still face challenges (1). Overall, the scheme improved living conditions significantly because it worked with the community, but it did not remove inequality, so improvement has been partial (1).
